paragraphs: Classification models often train with a smooth substitute for the error measure they ultimately care about. This paper studies mathematical bounds connecting progress on that substitute loss to progress on classification error. Its focus includes H-consistency bounds, which account for the particular family of predictors available to the learner.

For binary classification, the authors establish matching upper and lower square-root growth rates near zero for smooth margin-based losses, under mild assumptions. They also connect this result to excess error bounds. For multiclass classification, they establish the same type of rate for smooth comp-sum and constrained losses, including common neural-network training choices.

Sharing a growth rate does not make all these losses interchangeable. The paper examines how bounds depend on class count and, when constants are ignored near zero, identifies minimizability gaps as a key distinction. Its comparisons and conditions for zero or small gaps offer a theoretical basis for choosing among losses whose leading growth behavior looks similar.
neurips-2024-a-universal-growth-rate-for.tldr: The paper establishes square-root error-bound growth for several smooth classification losses and identifies minimizability gaps as a key factor distinguishing them.

paragraphs: When several players learn while interacting, each player's decisions change the situation faced by the others. This paper asks whether momentum, inspired by accelerated methods for convex optimization, can also speed learning in finite games. It develops a family of methods called follow the accelerated leader, or FTXL.

FTXL adds momentum to regularized learning, including exponential and multiplicative weights methods. The authors use ideas from continuous-time analyses of Nesterov acceleration to study its behavior near strict Nash equilibria. These are strategy configurations where each player's equilibrium choice is strictly preferable to deviations when the other players' choices remain fixed.

The central guarantee is local: near such equilibria, FTXL converges at a superlinear rate, yielding an exponential speed-up over the geometric convergence of ordinary regularized learning. The result extends across several feedback settings, including stochastic observations and bandit feedback where players see only their own realized payoffs. Thus, the acceleration is not confined to players who receive complete information.
neurips-2024-accelerated-regularized-lea.tldr: FTXL adds momentum to regularized game learning and achieves faster local convergence to strict Nash equilibria across several feedback settings.

paragraphs: Learning policies for interacting agents can require many experiences and transfer poorly to new situations. This paper investigates whether building spatial symmetry into the policy network can help. Its starting point is an equivariant graph neural network, whose behavior respects rotations, translations, and reflections of the nodes representing a multi-agent situation.

The authors find that this structure improves sample efficiency and generalization, but also exposes a problem: a straightforward application can bias early behavior and weaken exploration. They introduce Exploration-enhanced Equivariant Graph Neural Networks, or E2GN2, to mitigate this architectural bias while retaining the benefits of symmetry.

Evaluations on MPE and SMACv2 compare E2GN2 with common alternatives for representing learned functions. The reported results include significant improvements in sample efficiency, higher final reward convergence, and gains of two to five times over standard graph neural networks in the generalization tests. The findings show why useful structural assumptions must also be considered in relation to exploration: a network can encode valuable symmetry while still needing help discovering rewarding behavior.
neurips-2024-boosting-sample-efficiency-.tldr: E2GN2 combines spatial symmetry with improved exploration to increase sample efficiency and generalization in tested multi-agent learning tasks.

paragraphs: Producing language models at several sizes usually means paying for several training runs from scratch. This paper investigates a different route: remove parts of an existing model, then retrain the smaller model using less than three percent of the original training data. Knowledge distillation guides that retraining using the larger model.

The authors empirically examine pruning along several dimensions: depth, width, attention, and multilayer perceptron components. They also investigate how to combine these choices, select compressed architectures, and apply distillation. The resulting practical guidance is used to shrink models in the Nemotron-4 family by factors of two to four.

On the evaluated language tasks, the compressed models outperform Nemotron-3 8B and LLaMa2 7B with up to forty times fewer training tokens. They match Mistral 7B and Gemma 7B with up to eighty-five times fewer tokens, while slightly trailing LLaMa3 8B with up to 159 times fewer tokens. These comparisons support compression and limited retraining as a promising way to derive smaller models from an already trained foundation.
neurips-2024-compact-language-models-via.tldr: Pruning and distillation produce compact Nemotron-4 models that compete with similarly sized models using substantially fewer retraining tokens.

paragraphs: Synthetic data may help protect privacy, but statistical conclusions drawn from them can differ from conclusions drawn from the original observations. This paper studies bias and uncertainty introduced by deep generative models. The issue can affect even simple quantities such as means, making uncertainty shrink more slowly than the familiar inverse-square-root sample-size rate.

That slower convergence matters because confidence intervals and p-values depend on understanding an estimator's uncertainty. The authors propose tailoring synthetic-data generation to a specific intended analysis. Drawing on debiased and targeted machine learning, their strategy accounts for bias, improves convergence rates, and produces estimators whose large-sample variances can be approximated readily.

The paper illustrates the approach with a toy-data simulation and two real-world case studies. Its central contribution is to connect how synthetic data are generated with the statistical question those data will answer. The findings support analysis-specific tailoring as a way to improve inferential reliability, rather than treating the usefulness of synthetic data as independent of their eventual analytical purpose.
neurips-2024-debiasing-synthetic-data-ge.tldr: Tailoring deep generative models to specific statistical analyses can reduce synthetic-data bias and improve uncertainty estimation.

paragraphs: Differentially private training modifies learning updates to protect information about training data. Common optimizers clip gradients and add privacy noise, but the resulting models can lose substantial predictive performance. This paper approaches that trade-off through signal processing, asking whether the useful learning signal can be strengthened relative to the added noise.

The authors define a frequency-domain view of both gradients and privacy noise. They introduce DOPPLER, a low-pass filtering component for private optimizers, that amplifies the gradient signal while suppressing the impact of noise in that representation. The method is designed to retain the privacy guarantees of the training procedure while improving the learned model.

Across the models and datasets evaluated, optimizers equipped with the filter outperform their corresponding versions without it. The paper also provides theoretical evidence for the approach. Together, these results support filtering as a way to narrow the performance gap between private and non-private training, while keeping privacy protection part of the optimization process.
neurips-2024-doppler-differentially-priv.tldr: DOPPLER uses low-pass filtering to reduce the impact of privacy noise and improve private training while preserving privacy guarantees.

paragraphs: Many learning systems represent objects as points whose distances encode comparisons. This paper asks how many coordinates are needed to represent such information. It studies contrastive examples, where a positive must be closer to an anchor than a negative, and nearest-neighbor information, where each point has an ordered list of nearby points.

The analysis connects these questions to the arboricity of associated graphs, a property describing their decomposition into forests. For Euclidean distance, it obtains matching upper and lower bounds: square-root growth in the number of contrastive samples, and linear growth in k for preserving the ordering of k neighbors. These characterize the dimensions sufficient in general and necessary in the worst case.

The paper also gives bounds for other distance norms and extends contrastive results to multiple negatives. It distinguishes preserving the ordering of specified neighbors from additionally ensuring they remain the nearest neighbors among all points. That distinction matters because these are different representation requirements, and the authors provide a separate sufficiency result for the stronger one.
neurips-2024-embedding-dimension-of-cont.tldr: Graph structure yields tight Euclidean dimension bounds for representing contrastive comparisons and ordered nearest-neighbor information.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces a language model's memory requirements by representing weights with lower precision. This paper examines a security consequence: an attacker can construct a model that appears benign at full precision but exhibits deliberately injected harmful behavior after quantization. The concern is a mismatch between the version inspected and the version ultimately deployed.

The demonstrated framework first creates a model with adversarial behavior. It then identifies the set of full-precision weights that quantize to that malicious model. By adjusting weights within those constraints, the authors remove the poisoned behavior from the full-precision version while preserving what the quantized version will become.

Experiments demonstrate this possibility for vulnerable code generation, content injection, and excessive refusal. The authors also describe a possible distribution route through a public model hub, where users could download the apparently benign model and quantize it themselves. The findings establish a concrete attack mechanism under the tested methods: benign behavior before compression does not by itself establish benign behavior after the transformation.
neurips-2024-exploiting-llm-quantization.tldr: The paper demonstrates models whose deliberately hidden adversarial behavior emerges after quantization despite benign behavior at full precision.

paragraphs: Online class incremental learning asks a model to learn from successive small batches as new classes arrive, without access to earlier data. A central difficulty is forgetting previously learned knowledge. Storing examples for replay can help, but uses extra memory; methods that avoid storing examples often sacrifice accuracy.

F-OAL combines a pretrained, frozen encoder with feature fusion and an analytically updated linear classifier. The encoder supplies representations while recursive least squares updates the classifier. Because this process does not rely on backpropagation, it reduces the memory and computation associated with training. It also avoids retaining examples for replay in production.

Experiments on benchmark datasets report robust performance in the online class incremental setting, combining high accuracy with low resource consumption. The approach matters because it changes which part of the model must keep learning: a fixed representation supports a classifier that can be updated as batches arrive. The stated results show that this combination can offer a favorable balance between retaining knowledge and limiting training resources.
neurips-2024-f-oal-forward-only-online-a.tldr: F-OAL combines frozen features with recursive classifier updates to support accurate, resource-efficient incremental learning without replay or backpropagation.

paragraphs: A dataset's topological structure describes aspects of its shape across scales. Persistent homology provides a way to summarize such structure, but using more than one scale parameter usually creates substantial theoretical and computational difficulty. This paper introduces graphcodes for data examined along two real-valued scale parameters.

A graphcode packages the resulting multiscale information as an embedded graph. The authors describe it as informative and interpretable, with computation as efficient as that of one-parameter summaries. Its graph form also creates a direct connection to graph neural networks, allowing the topological summary to become an input to a learning system.

The paper develops this integration into a classification pipeline and reports higher accuracy than state-of-the-art alternatives on several datasets. The contribution therefore spans both representation and use: it makes two-parameter topological information more practical to compute and supplies a familiar machine-learning structure for processing it. The classification results provide empirical support that this representation preserves information useful for distinguishing examples in the evaluated datasets.
neurips-2024-graphcode-learning-from-mul.tldr: Graphcodes turn two-parameter topological summaries into efficiently computed graphs that improve classification in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: An image-editing model must respond to an instruction while producing an acceptable edited image. Evaluating that outcome involves several aspects of quality, so a single overall impression can conceal useful differences between systems. I2EBench provides an automated benchmark intended to assess instruction-based image editing across multiple dimensions.

The benchmark contains more than 2,000 input images and more than 4,000 diverse editing instructions. Its sixteen evaluation dimensions cover both high-level and low-level aspects of results. The authors also conduct a user study for each dimension to examine alignment with human perception, connecting the automated evaluation to how people judge the edits.

By comparing existing models across these dimensions, the paper identifies strengths and weaknesses intended to guide further research. The described release includes instructions, inputs, human annotations, outputs from evaluated models, and a script for assessing new results. This combination supports more detailed comparisons: researchers can examine where an editing model succeeds or struggles, rather than relying only on an undifferentiated quality judgment.
neurips-2024-i2ebench-a-comprehensive-be.tldr: I2EBench evaluates instruction-based image editing across sixteen dimensions, supported by diverse instructions and human-perception studies.

paragraphs: ProtoViT classifies images by comparing them with learned prototypes, making its reasoning expressible through visual resemblance. Instead of providing only a class prediction, this approach ties the decision to recognizable comparison features. The paper combines this case-based reasoning with a vision transformer backbone.

The prototypes consist of parts whose spatial arrangement can deform to fit irregular object geometry. Their number of parts is also adaptive. This addresses a limitation of spatially rigid prototypes: corresponding features in two images may occupy different arrangements. Flexible parts are intended to preserve coherent comparisons while accommodating those geometric differences.

The authors report that ProtoViT generally achieves higher performance than existing prototype-based models. They also analyze prototype consistency and the faithfulness of the resulting interpretations. These findings matter together because the method seeks useful predictions and explanations grounded in the comparisons the model actually makes. The contribution is a way to make prototype reasoning more adaptable to object variation while retaining clear visual representations of the evidence used for classification.
neurips-2024-interpretable-image-classif.tldr: ProtoViT combines vision transformers with deformable, adaptive prototypes to improve image classification while explaining decisions through visual comparisons.

paragraphs: Generating very large images puts pressure on GPU memory because the model must process a large spatial representation. Pixelsmith addresses this problem with a zero-shot framework that extends a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model to higher resolutions. The authors demonstrate output scaling by a factor of 1,000, pointing toward gigapixel generation.

The method works in stages, using a low-resolution generated image as the starting guide for larger images. A mechanism called the Slider combines the overall structure of that first image with finer detail. During each inference step, the framework denoises patches instead of the complete latent representation, reducing the memory demands of processing the image.

This patch-based design is presented as enabling a single GPU to handle the process regardless of image resolution. Experiments report better image quality and diversity than existing techniques, together with shorter sampling times and fewer artifacts. The approach connects global guidance with local computation: the initial image supplies overall organization while patch processing makes higher-resolution generation more manageable.
neurips-2024-is-one-gpu-enough-pushing-i.tldr: Pixelsmith combines cascading guidance and patchwise denoising to scale pretrained image generation to much higher resolutions on one GPU.

paragraphs: Learning garment animation directly from many examples of moving garments requires expensive data collection. It can also tie a model too closely to the motions it has observed. This paper separates learning how cloth responds to deformation from using that knowledge to animate garments of different forms.

Its Energy Unit network, EUNet, learns constitutive behavior from the observed motion of a piece of cloth. It represents changes caused by deformations, including stretching and bending, in terms of energy. The method learns these relations without priors from analytical physics models or differentiable simulation engines. A pretrained EUNet then constrains garment animation through energy optimization.

This separation allows dynamics learned from a piece of cloth to support animation of various garments, reducing the need for garment-specific training data. Experiments show that EUNet supplies useful deformation-related energy gradients and that models constrained by it produce more stable, physically plausible behavior than garment-wise supervised models. The findings support learning reusable material behavior as an alternative to matching complete garment trajectories directly.
neurips-2024-learning-3d-garment-animati.tldr: EUNet learns deformation energy from a piece of cloth and uses it to support more stable, physically plausible garment animation.

paragraphs: Plaintext-ciphertext matching can be represented as a Boolean satisfiability problem. However, the conjunctive normal form used by existing neural SAT solvers can represent cryptographic operations inefficiently, particularly XOR, and obscure their higher-level structure. This paper develops an ANF-based graph representation to address that bottleneck.

The representation handles XOR operations compactly and includes a dedicated encoding for AND operations. CryptoANFNet then passes messages through this graph to classify whether plaintext-ciphertext conditions are satisfiable. The authors argue that the representation improves scalability while retaining information about higher-order operations. They also introduce a key-solving algorithm that simplifies these instances.

In the reported experiments, CryptoANFNet is fifty times faster than heuristic solvers. Its accuracy exceeds NeuroSAT's on both small-scale datasets, 96% versus 91%, and large-scale datasets, 72% versus 55%. The key-solving method also improves accuracy on datasets from two encryption algorithms. These results support the value of preserving cryptographic operation structure when building learned solvers for the evaluated problems.
neurips-2024-learning-plaintext-cipherte.tldr: CryptoANFNet uses ANF-based graphs to represent cryptographic SAT problems more effectively, improving reported speed, scalability, and prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: A policy decision can benefit different people by different amounts. A social welfare function combines those individual utilities into a judgment about the group. This paper asks whether observed judgments can reveal the rule a policymaker uses, focusing on the established family of power mean functions.

The authors study two kinds of evidence. In one setting, each vector of individual utilities comes with a numerical welfare judgment. In the other, the learner receives comparisons indicating which of two utility vectors has higher welfare. These settings distinguish learning from explicit scores from learning through relative preferences.

For both tasks, the paper proves learnability with polynomial sample complexity, including when the welfare information contains noise. It also develops practical algorithms and evaluates their performance. The result gives a formal basis for recovering this class of aggregation rules from observations. Its scope is the specified power mean family, so the contribution concerns learning a structured model of a policymaker's judgments rather than establishing that arbitrary decision rationales can be recovered.
neurips-2024-learning-social-welfare-fun.tldr: Power mean social welfare functions can be learned from numerical judgments or pairwise comparisons with polynomial sample complexity, even under noise.

paragraphs: When a trained model encounters shifted data, its accuracy may change even though no labels are available to measure that change. MaNo estimates accuracy from the model's output scores, or logits. The paper addresses a weakness of existing logit-based methods: overconfidence can bias their estimates, particularly under natural distribution shifts.

The authors first examine logits and generalization through the low-density separation assumption. That analysis motivates a data-dependent normalization designed to reduce prediction bias. MaNo then gathers the normalized logits into a matrix and uses its Lp norm as an estimation score. The theoretical analysis connects this score to model uncertainty.

An extensive evaluation on unsupervised accuracy-estimation benchmarks reports state-of-the-art performance across different architectures and synthetic, natural, and subpopulation shifts. The method matters because it extracts an accuracy signal from outputs already available at prediction time. Its contribution combines a normalization step addressing overconfidence with a matrix-level summary, and the experiments support that combination across the tested forms of distribution change.
neurips-2024-mano-exploiting-matrix-norm.tldr: MaNo estimates accuracy without labels by normalizing model logits and measuring their matrix norm, improving results across tested distribution shifts.

paragraphs: In constrained online convex optimization, a learner chooses an action before seeing that round's cost and constraint functions. It must keep both regret and accumulated constraint violations small, even when an adaptive adversary determines what it encounters. The challenge is to control these two quantities simultaneously across a sequence of T rounds.

The paper presents a simple first-order policy achieving regret of order square root of T and cumulative constraint violation of the same order up to logarithmic factors. The authors establish this without the restrictive assumptions that had left the simultaneous guarantee an open question. Their method combines adaptive online optimization policies with Lyapunov optimization from control theory.

When the cost functions are strongly convex and the constraints remain convex, the regret guarantee improves to logarithmic growth while the constraint-violation bound stays the same. These results matter because both accumulated quantities grow sublinearly with the horizon. The method therefore provides simultaneous long-run control of decision quality and constraint violations, with a stronger performance guarantee under additional cost curvature.
neurips-2024-optimal-algorithms-for-onli.tldr: A first-order online policy simultaneously achieves square-root-scale regret and constraint violations, with logarithmic regret under strongly convex costs.

paragraphs: A single weather prediction describes one possible future, but the chaotic nature of weather makes uncertainty part of the forecasting problem. Graph-EFM produces probabilistic forecasts by combining a latent-variable model with a graph-based forecasting framework. This allows the model to generate an ensemble of possible weather outcomes.

The model uses a hierarchical graph to sample forecasts that remain spatially coherent. That coherence matters because a forecast describes a connected weather field rather than a collection of unrelated local values. Each time step requires only one forward pass, supporting fast generation of ensembles with arbitrarily many members.

The authors evaluate Graph-EFM on both global forecasts and forecasts for a limited geographic area. Its ensemble forecasts achieve errors equivalent to or lower than comparable deterministic models while also capturing forecast uncertainty accurately. The reported findings show that probabilistic modeling can add information about possible outcomes without worsening the evaluated forecast errors. The architecture's efficient sampling also makes generating many alternative futures a central part of the forecasting process.
neurips-2024-probabilistic-weather-forec.tldr: Graph-EFM efficiently generates coherent weather ensembles that capture uncertainty while matching or improving on comparable deterministic forecast errors.

paragraphs: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a pretrained model by learning a small update while keeping its original weights fixed. Such methods can save trainable parameters but often trail full fine-tuning. SVFT addresses this trade-off by constructing each update from the singular vectors of the particular weight matrix being adapted.

The update is a sparse combination of outer products of these vectors, with only the combination coefficients trained. Crucially, SVFT allows selected off-diagonal coefficients to change as well. This gives the method a way to increase expressivity gradually by making more coefficients learnable, connecting the parameter budget directly to the update's flexibility.

Across language and vision benchmarks, the authors report recovery of up to 96% of full fine-tuning performance while training 0.006% to 0.25% of parameters. The compared methods reach up to 85% with larger reported parameter fractions. These empirical results support adapting updates to the structure of existing weights as a useful route toward stronger performance with very few trainable parameters.
neurips-2024-svft-parameter-efficient-fi.tldr: SVFT learns sparse combinations of a model's singular vectors, recovering up to 96% of full fine-tuning performance with few trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Strong language-modeling results do not fully explain which computations an architecture can represent in principle. This paper studies recurrent models based on linear state space models through formal-language theory. It compares their expressive capacity with transformers and traditional recurrent neural networks to clarify where their strengths overlap and differ.

For star-free state-tracking problems, the authors find straightforward, exact solutions using state space models where transformers struggle with exact representation. They also show that these models can represent bounded hierarchical structure using optimal memory, without needing to simulate a stack. These results identify concrete computational abilities behind the architecture's sequential processing.

The study also identifies a design choice in current state space models that restricts expressive power. Its picture is therefore one of distinct architectural strengths and constraints, rather than a single overall ranking. Empirical tests on Mamba verify the theoretical results. The findings provide guidance for architecture research by connecting particular design decisions to the types of state tracking and structured sequences a model can express.
neurips-2024-the-expressive-capacity-of-.tldr: A formal-language analysis identifies state space models' strengths in state tracking and bounded hierarchy, alongside a design-related expressivity limit.

paragraphs: Scaffold hopping searches for related candidate molecules by changing their core structure. It narrows the enormous chemical search space while seeking compounds with useful activity. TurboHopp combines this strategy with three-dimensional generation conditioned on a binding pocket, addressing the slow processing of existing structure-based generative approaches.

The model uses consistency models to accelerate molecule generation while accounting for the pocket and molecular geometry. The authors report inference speeds up to thirty times faster than existing diffusion-based models, together with better generation quality. Faster generation is central to the approach because it reduces the time required to produce candidate molecular structures.

The paper then uses Reinforcement Learning for Consistency Models to further optimize generation toward desirable molecules. It demonstrates the approach across multiple drug-discovery scenarios, supporting its potential across different molecular settings. The contribution joins a focused search strategy with rapid generation and subsequent optimization: scaffold hopping defines the type of structural change being explored, while the generative model makes that exploration faster.
neurips-2024-turbohopp-accelerated-molec.tldr: TurboHopp uses consistency models for pocket-conditioned scaffold hopping, reporting up to thirtyfold faster inference and improved molecular generation quality.

paragraphs: Assessing a language model's moral consistency requires distinguishing its judgments from biases in how it selects answers. This paper studies symmetric moral consistency in twelve popular language models. It finds that measured consistency scores are affected by position and selection biases, complicating their interpretation as evidence of the models' underlying abilities.

The authors introduce tSMC, a framework that measures these bias effects and mitigates their influence using Kullback–Leibler divergence. Its purpose is to make the assessment more informative about consistency after accounting for these response tendencies. This addresses the measurement process as well as the models being measured.

The resulting investigation finds that consistency depends on the moral scenario. Across the twelve models, average scores range from 60.7% for highly ambiguous scenarios to 84.8% for low-ambiguity scenarios. Models are more consistent when a clear moral answer exists than when every option has a moral drawback. These findings connect weaker consistency to ambiguity while showing why raw response scores need careful treatment when answer biases affect the evaluation.
neurips-2024-unveiling-the-bias-impact-o.tldr: tSMC mitigates answer biases in moral-consistency evaluation and finds lower consistency among twelve language models in more ambiguous scenarios.

paragraphs: Domain-specific languages can make specialized software clearer and more efficient, but adopting them often requires rewriting existing programs. Language models can help translate code, yet their translations alone do not guarantee that behavior is preserved. Verified lifting addresses this problem by seeking target programs that are functionally equivalent to the source.

LLMLift uses language models both to translate programs and to generate proofs of functional equivalence. The approach combines their program-reasoning capabilities with the objective of verified lifting. It aims to reduce the specialization and domain expertise required by earlier synthesis-based tools, whose search procedures can be difficult to build for new language pairs.

The authors develop lifting-based compilers for four domain-specific languages across different application areas. Their approach translates more benchmark programs and takes less transpilation time than previous symbolic tools, while requiring substantially less construction effort. The contribution is therefore both a translation approach and a method for building verified translators: generating equivalence proofs is part of the workflow for establishing that rewritten code preserves the original computation.
neurips-2024-verified-code-transpilation.tldr: LLMLift uses language models to translate programs and generate equivalence proofs, improving verified lifting across four domain-specific languages.

paragraphs: Learning useful representations for tables has attracted attention, but databases containing several related tables remain less explored. One obstacle is the shortage of open resources for training and studying such systems. WikiDBs addresses this need with an open-source collection of 100,000 relational databases derived from Wikidata.

Each database contains multiple tables connected through foreign keys, which express relationships between records in different tables. The collection is designed to reflect selected characteristics of real-world databases. The paper describes both the resource and its construction method, making the generation process part of the contribution alongside the resulting data.

Publicly available code allows researchers to create tailored variants, including databases in different languages. Initial experiments illustrate training for missing-value imputation and column-type annotation. These demonstrations show concrete uses for the corpus rather than establishing a universal advantage for a particular model. The broader purpose is to provide material for developing foundation models that can learn from tables together with the relationships connecting them.
neurips-2024-wikidbs-a-large-scale-corpu.tldr: WikiDBs supplies 100,000 connected, multitable databases and generation code to support learning for relational data and data-engineering tasks.
